container: The gig economy describes a labor market where people earn income through short term jobs, freelance projects, or services arranged through platforms. Instead of working for one employer on a schedule, gig workers may choose when, where, and how much they work. Examples include driving passengers, delivering food, designing websites, tutoring, and renting out a room. This model can offer flexibility. It can help workers balance jobs with caregiving, studies, or other interests, and allow businesses to find help when demand changes. Platforms make it easy to connect customers and workers, handle payments, and review services. However, gig work also brings uncertainty. Earnings may vary from week to week, and workers can face costs for equipment, transportation, insurance, and taxes. Many do not receive paid leave, employer sponsored health coverage, or retirement benefits. Platform rules and ratings can affect access to jobs, while workers may have limited ways to challenge decisions. Understanding the gig economy means considering independence and risk. Contracts, fair pay, portable benefits, and transparent platform policies can improve conditions. Governments, companies, and workers continue to debate how labor protections should adapt as this form of work grows.
